title: Alternating Series and the Error Bound

steps.body:
The harmonic series diverges. But put a **minus sign on every other term** —

1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + …

— and it converges, to ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

The terms have not changed size at all. Only their signs. Convergence is not just about how fast terms fade; it is about **cancellation**.

explanationVariants: Each partial sum overshoots, then undershoots, then overshoots by less — the sums BOUNCE and close in on a limit, squeezed between consecutive partial sums.
S₁ = 1, S₂ = 0.5, S₃ = 0.833, S₄ = 0.583 — the interval is halving in on ln 2 ≈ 0.693 from both sides.

widget.prompt: The partial sums of 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … run 1, 0.5, 0.833, 0.583, … What are they doing?

options.label: Bouncing above and below, and closing in — each step is smaller than the last, so they squeeze onto a limit.
options.feedback: Right, and the limit is trapped BETWEEN any two consecutive partial sums. That is what makes the error so easy to bound.

options.label: Growing without bound, like the harmonic series.
options.feedback: The harmonic series climbs monotonically. These sums bounce, and each bounce is smaller — they are being squeezed onto ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

options.label: Oscillating forever without settling.
options.feedback: They would, if the terms did not FADE. Because the steps shrink to zero, the bouncing closes in rather than continuing forever.

options.label: Converging to 0.5.
options.feedback: 0.5 is only S₂. The sums continue past it and settle on ln 2 ≈ 0.693.

widget.prompt: Why the error is so easy to bound here.

panels.title: Each step overshoots
panels.body: Add +1/3 and you go past the limit. Subtract 1/4 and you fall back below it. Every partial sum lands on the OPPOSITE side of the limit from the last one.

panels.title: So the limit is trapped
panels.body: If S₃ is above and S₄ is below, the true sum is somewhere between them. And the gap between S₃ and S₄ is exactly the size of the term you just added: 1/4.

panels.title: The error bound
panels.body: So the error after n terms is smaller than the FIRST TERM YOU LEFT OUT. Not roughly — provably. That is the cleanest error bound in the whole subject, and it costs nothing to compute.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is a theorem, not a rule of thumb.
widget.successFeedback: The limit is trapped between consecutive partial sums, so the error is smaller than the first omitted term. Free, and exact.

explanationVariants: Stop after 4 terms and the first omitted term is 1/5 = 0.2. So the error is less than 0.2 — no calculation of the true sum required.
You get an error bound for free, just by looking at the next term you did not add.

widget.prompt: For 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + …, you stop after 4 terms. What is the largest the error can be?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the term you DID add (1/4). The bound is the FIRST OMITTED term, which is 1/5 = 0.2.
That is S₄, the partial sum itself, not the error in it. The error is bounded by the next term: 1/5.
That is the true limit, ln 2. The error bound is the first omitted term, 1/5 = 0.2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The first omitted term is 1/5 = 0.2, so the error is smaller than that.

steps.body:
The test itself has two conditions, and both are needed:

**The terms must alternate in sign.**
**Their SIZES must shrink, steadily, to zero.**

If either fails, the bouncing does not close in — and the series need not converge at all.
How many terms for two decimals?
explanationVariants: You need the first omitted term under 0.01: 1/(n + 1) < 0.01 gives n + 1 > 100, so n = 100 terms.
That is a lot of terms for two decimal places — alternating series converge, but this one converges VERY slowly.

widget.prompt: For 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − …, how many terms are needed to guarantee an error below 0.01?

commonErrors.feedback: The bound is 1/(n + 1) < 0.01, which needs n + 1 > 100. Ten terms leaves an error of up to 1/11 ≈ 0.09 — ten times too big.
Close: 1/(n + 1) < 0.01 needs n + 1 > 100, so n = 100. With n = 99 the bound is exactly 0.01, which is not strictly less.
Two terms leaves an error of up to 1/3 ≈ 0.33.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 1/(n + 1) < 0.01 → n = 100 terms. Convergent, but painfully slow.

steps.body: Bound an error you cannot compute.
hints: Stop after 3 terms. What is the FIRST term you left out?
explanationVariants: The first omitted term is 1/16 = 0.0625, so the error after 3 terms is smaller than that.
You bounded the error of a series whose sum you have never computed and could not easily name. That is what the theorem buys you.

widget.prompt: For 1 − 1/4 + 1/9 − 1/16 + …, you stop after 3 terms. Bound the error, to four decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 1/9 — the term you DID add. The bound is the first term you LEFT OUT, which is 1/16.
That is 1/36, the FIFTH term. You stopped after three, so the first omitted one is the fourth: 1/16.
That is the partial sum 1 − 1/4 + 1/9, not the error in it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The first omitted term is 1/16 = 0.0625, so the error is smaller than that.

steps.body: Cancellation, and a free error bound.
takeaways: Alternating signs can rescue a series whose terms fade too slowly to be summed on their own.
The partial sums bounce and close in, so the limit is trapped BETWEEN consecutive partial sums.
Hence the error is smaller than the FIRST OMITTED TERM — provably, and for free.
steps.teaser: Last: differentiate and integrate a series term by term, and get new ones for nothing.

concept.body: Add a term and you overshoot. Subtract the next and you fall short. Each step is smaller than the last, so the sums close in from both sides — and the true limit is always caught between the last two. That is why the error is never bigger than the next term you would have added.

explanationVariants: Stopping after 5 terms leaves 1/6 as the first omitted one, so the error is under 1/6 ≈ 0.167.
The bound is always the next term you did not add.

widget.prompt: For 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − …, stop after 5 terms. Bound the error, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 1/5 — the term you DID add. The first OMITTED one is 1/6 ≈ 0.167.
That is the partial sum, not the error in it.
